title: 2 Rooks VS 2 Pawns
summary: Use checking tempos to build a blockade and gain time for the king, then answer either promotion.

nodes.question: Can Black blockade both advanced pawns in time?
nodes.explanation: Black has Kb8, Ra1 and Rd6 against Kf2, g7 and h6. Black moves first and must displace the white king with check.

nodes.question: Does a knight promotion change the finish?
nodes.explanation: This separately reviewed late source diagram has Kf7/g7/h7 against Kf5/Rc8/Rd8. The intervening repeated king walk is source context rather than an invented connecting sequence.

branches.title: Check, blockade and gain a king tempo
commentary: Begin with Black to move in the complete six-piece source root.
Rd2+ forces the king away from the first two ranks before the rooks take up the blockade.
Ke3 is the selected king escape from check, moving from f2 to e3.
Rd8 moves the checking rook to the back rank.
h7 brings the pawns side by side on the seventh rank.
Re1+ uses the other rook to gain a checking tempo.
Kf4 is the illustrated king response.
Re8 completes the back-rank blockade. Capturing a promoted piece can be followed by the other rook’s recapture.
Kf5 tries to approach the rooks and pawns.
Rc8 makes room for the other rook to switch files.
Kf6 advances toward the blockade.
Rd8 shifts the other rook behind the approaching king.
Kf7 reaches the seventh rank.
Rd7+ checks horizontally and pushes the king away.
Kf6 retreats one rank.
Rd6+ checks again and denies the king its previous position.
Ke5 is the selected retreat, preserving White’s most resilient route in the narration.
Rd8 restores the blockade while the king is farther away.
Kf6 approaches again, but now it takes another move to reach f7.
Kb7 spends that extra tempo improving Black’s king. The exact position remains a Black win; the repeated later king walk is not encoded as an uninterrupted sequence.
branches.explanation: Kb7 spends that extra tempo improving Black’s king. The exact position remains a Black win; the repeated later king walk is not encoded as an uninterrupted sequence.

branches.title: Blockade without checking first
commentary: Compare the source’s passive blockade before displacing Kf2.
Rd8 gives up Black’s forced win, but the exact position is drawn at this point; the later ...Rh1 mistake will lose.
h7 threatens both promotions and preserves the draw against best defense.
Rh1 tries to stop the h-pawn, but this is the losing error: the g-pawn can promote with a winning recapture.
g8=Q creates a queen while the white king remains safe on f2.
Rxg8 removes that queen but places the rook on the h-pawn’s capture square.
hxg8=Q promotes by recapture. White retains a checked win against the remaining rook.
branches.explanation: hxg8=Q promotes by recapture. White retains a checked win against the remaining rook.

branches.title: A queen promotion allows mate
commentary: Begin in the separately reviewed late six-piece diagram after ...Kf5, not at the initial root.
g8=Q creates a queen but cannot save the king.
Rc7# is actual mate. Kf5 controls e6/f6/g6, Rd8 controls the eighth rank and the checking rook seals rank seven.
branches.explanation: Rc7# is actual mate. Kf5 controls e6/f6/g6, Rd8 controls the eighth rank and the checking rook seals rank seven.

branches.title: A knight promotion blocks with check
commentary: Compare the source’s more resilient knight underpromotion in the same late diagram.
g8=N creates a knight that can interpose with check on e7.
Rc7+ checks, but the knight means this is not mate.
Ne7+ blocks the rook check while attacking Kf5.
Rxe7+ captures that knight and answers its check with a check.
Kxe7 takes the sacrificed rook, leaving a rook against the last pawn.
Rh8 stops h8 promotion from behind. This is a checked Black win, requiring normal conversion rather than an immediate mate.
branches.explanation: Rh8 stops h8 promotion from behind. This is a checked Black win, requiring normal conversion rather than an immediate mate.

exercises.prompt: Why check before building the blockade?
exercises.answer: The check pushes the white king away before the rooks move behind the pawns. Later rank checks force another retreat and gain time to improve Black’s king.

exercises.prompt: Why is the knight promotion different?
exercises.answer: It blocks Rc7+ with Ne7+, giving check itself. Black must capture that knight before stopping the remaining h-pawn.

startContext: Black plays from the complete six-piece root. A checked opening blockade sequence ends after ...Kb7. A separately reconstructed late diagram after ...Kf5 checks both promotion choices; the source’s repeated intervening king walk remains context, with no invented connection.
verification_scope: Saved board images reviewed manually. Every encoded intermediate position and endpoint is checked against the tablebase. Selected instructive variations, not an exhaustive tree of all legal defenses.
sourceCorrections: In the exact root, the passive ...Rd8 h7 comparison is drawn; it becomes a White win only after ...Rh1. The lesson distinguishes the drawing error from the later losing error.
